▶  Watch the case-study video The full walkthrough on YouTube — the research, the decisions, and the working build in motion.
壱The signal

A personal annoyance that turned out to be everyone's

It started the way a lot of usable products do — with a problem I was living. My reading habit was leaking; I'd finish a book and keep almost none of it. Before designing anything, I checked whether the pain was mine alone.

Those view counts weren't opinions — they were a crowd quietly raising their hands. The same question, asked by millions, across unrelated creators. My private frustration was a widespread, under-served need. That was the green light.

弐The incumbent

The existing tool didn't earn the effort it asked for

Someone had tried to solve this — I found Readwise and genuinely wanted it to be the answer. The value was there in theory, but the experience cost more than it returned. Rather than trust my own reaction, I interviewed nine people from the target audience.

The complaints clustered: a flow that felt heavier than the payoff justified. I stopped guessing and documented every friction point users hit as they moved through it. That list became my brief.

参The advantage

I didn't let the design die as a clickable prototype

Instead of handing over a static mockup and waiting, I designed the app and then rebuilt it as a functioning one — not a mockup pretending to work, but something I could put in a hand and watch get used.

That changed my feedback loop entirely. People stopped imagining how a flow would feel and started tapping through it — failing and succeeding at the exact friction points I'd catalogued.

四The iteration

Two full cycles — the surviving version, not a lucky guess

I re-interviewed, redesigned, re-interviewed and redesigned again — two complete cycles, each grounded in watching real behaviour rather than my own taste. The capture flow got simpler; the recall surface got tuned until reviewing felt lighter than the reading it came from.

The final design wasn't my first idea. It was what was left after the weak ones got tested out.

五The takeaway

The pixels were never the job

The design file stayed the source of truth and I stayed the design authority — AI was just a faster brush. The real job was noticing a genuine pain, proving the demand behind it, refusing a tool that didn't deserve its users, and iterating against real reactions until the product fit. That's the same loop I run on client work — and the one I'd bring to your team.

Why full-time,
why now?

Honestly: freelancing resets every eight weeks. New client, new context, new codebase — and just as the work gets interesting, the contract ends. Teams compound. Freelance doesn't.

I want to stay with one product long enough to see a decision play out across releases — to own a design system, watch retention move, and be measured on outcomes instead of deliverables. A stable role gives me that depth; it gives you a designer who already knows how to operate without hand-holding from day one.

And I want to do it in India. This ecosystem has 2.3 lakh+ recognised startups and 100+ unicorns, yet most teams still ship with fewer than one designer per twenty developers. The outliers show what closing that gap is worth: Zerodha grew past a crore of customers with zero rupees of ad spend — the product did the marketing — and McKinsey found companies that treat design as seriously as engineering grow revenue 32 percentage points faster over five years. That's the gap I want to close for one Indian team.

三

The way I work 道

壱

Pain before pixels

I don't design a screen until I can name the specific friction it removes. If I can't, it doesn't earn its place in the build.

弐

Test, then trust

My taste is a hypothesis, not a verdict. I put flows in front of real users early and let what they do — not what they say — settle the argument.

参

Buildable by design

An engineering background means I think in constraints. I'd rather ship a feasible v1 this sprint than a perfect v3 that never leaves the file.
